\chapter{Describing an Experience --- How It Felt, How Long, How It Compared}
\label{ch:experiencia}
\hlchaptermodality{269}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say how something felt, what I hope for, how it compared with something else, and how long it lasted.}

Complete ES-C269-durante: describe one experience using a feeling adjective, an espero ambition, a mas que comparison, and a durante length.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[feliz]{feliz — happy, and an adjective that refuses to pick a gender}

\label{lesson:ES-C269-feliz}



\begin{quote}
You can say where things are and what has gone wrong. This chapter is about saying how it \emph{felt}. It starts with the most useful feeling word, which also happens to be conveniently lazy.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item problema — and the gender surprise it carried.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item Two syllables, stress on the last: \emph{fe-LIZ}. No written accent is needed — words ending in \emph{-z} are stressed on the final syllable by default. $\to$ reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{feliz} — \textquotedblleft{}happy.\textquotedblright{} Latin \emph{felix}, which first meant \textbf{fruitful} — of soil that bore a crop, of a tree heavy with fruit. Happiness, to a Roman farmer, was the field doing what it was supposed to do. The same \emph{felix} is the name \textbf{Felix}, and it is inside English \textbf{felicity}.

You already meet it once a year without translating it: \emph{¡feliz cumpleaños!}
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
\emph{Feliz} does something the adjectives you have met do not. \emph{Bueno} becomes \emph{buena} for a feminine noun; \emph{cansado} becomes \emph{cansada}. \emph{Feliz} does neither — it is \emph{feliz} for everyone. Adjectives ending in a consonant simply do not carry gender, so \emph{un niño feliz} and \emph{una niña feliz} use the identical word.

That is a saving, not an exception: every adjective you meet ending in \emph{-z}, \emph{-l} or \emph{-e} is one fewer form to remember.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{feliz} — stress the last syllable
  \item it about a man, then about a woman, and notice nothing changed
  \item \emph{¡feliz cumpleaños!}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What did Latin \emph{felix} first describe? (Fruitful soil, a fruiting tree.) Why does \emph{feliz} not change for a feminine noun? (It ends in a consonant, and consonant-final adjectives do not carry gender.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[espero viajar]{espero viajar — saying what you are reaching for}

\label{lesson:ES-C269-espero}



\begin{quote}
Ambitions are things you have not got yet. Spanish says them with a verb you have already met wearing a different coat.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item feliz — the feeling this chapter opened with.
  \item esperar — where you first met this verb, meaning \emph{wait}.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item Three syllables, stress in the middle: \emph{es-PE-ro}. $\to$ reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{espero} — \textquotedblleft{}I hope.\textquotedblright{} The same \emph{esperar} you learned as \textquotedblleft{}to wait,\textquotedblright{} and Spanish sees no reason to separate them. To wait for something and to hope for it are one act: you are standing in the present with your attention on a future you cannot reach yet.

\textbf{Where it comes from.} Latin \emph{sperare}, \textquotedblleft{}to hope\textquotedblright{} — the root of English \textbf{prosper} (\textquotedblleft{}to hope forward\textquotedblright{}) and, negated, \textbf{desperate}, which is literally \emph{de-sperare}, to have hope taken away. Spanish keeps the plain form; English kept the compounds.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
This is your ambition frame. \emph{Espero} plus an infinitive says what you are reaching for: \emph{espero viajar}, \emph{espero aprender}, \emph{espero vivir en España}. Every one of those infinitives is a verb you already own, so the frame costs you nothing new and turns your whole verb list into statements about your future.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{espero} — stress the middle
  \item an ambition — \emph{espero viajar}
  \item another, using any verb you know
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What two English meanings does \emph{esperar} carry? (To wait, and to hope.) What is \emph{desperate}, taken apart? (\emph{De-sperare} — hope taken away.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[más que]{más que — comparing two things, with no new endings to learn}

\label{lesson:ES-C269-mas-que}



\begin{quote}
English changes the adjective to compare: big, \emph{bigg-er}. Spanish refuses to. It puts one small word in front and leaves the adjective alone.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item espero — the ambition frame just before this.
  \item más — the degree word you already have.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{más} carries a written accent to keep it apart from \emph{mas}, an old word for \textquotedblleft{}but.\textquotedblright{} Two words, one sound, and the accent is the only thing telling them apart on the page. $\to$ reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{más que} — \textquotedblleft{}more than.\textquotedblright{} \emph{Más} (\textquotedblleft{}more\textquotedblright{}) plus \emph{que} (\textquotedblleft{}than,\textquotedblright{} and also \textquotedblleft{}that\textquotedblright{}).

\textbf{Where it comes from.} Latin \emph{magis}, \textquotedblleft{}more\textquotedblright{} — the same root as English \textbf{magnitude} and \textbf{major}. Latin \emph{did} have \emph{-ior} endings for comparison (\emph{maior}, \emph{melior}), exactly like English \emph{-er}. Spanish threw nearly all of them away and rebuilt comparison out of one adverb, which is why there is so little to learn here.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The pattern is fixed and takes any adjective you own, unchanged: \emph{más} + adjective + \emph{que}. \emph{Más grande que}, \emph{más feliz que}, \emph{más cansado que}. Swap \emph{más} for \emph{menos} and you have \textquotedblleft{}less than\textquotedblright{} for free.

Two words sit outside it, kept from Latin because they are used constantly: \emph{mejor} and \emph{peor}, \textquotedblleft{}better\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}worse\textquotedblright{} — as English says \emph{better}, not \emph{more good}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{más feliz que} — the adjective did not change
  \item the same idea downwards, with \emph{menos}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}better\textquotedblright{} without using \emph{más} (\emph{mejor})
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is the fixed pattern? (\emph{Más} + adjective + \emph{que}.) Why does \emph{más} carry an accent? (To separate it from \emph{mas}, \textquotedblleft{}but.\textquotedblright{}) Which two comparatives kept their Latin endings? (\emph{Mejor} and \emph{peor}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[durante]{durante — how long it lasted}

\label{lesson:ES-C269-durante}



\begin{quote}
An experience has a length. This is the word that gives it one, and it closes the chapter: you can now say how it felt, what you hope for, how it compared, and how long it went on.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item más que — the comparison just before this.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item Three syllables, stress in the middle: \emph{du-RAN-te}. $\to$ reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{durante} — \textquotedblleft{}during,\textquotedblright{} and often English \textquotedblleft{}for\textquotedblright{} when you are talking about a stretch of time: \emph{durante dos horas}, \textquotedblleft{}for two hours.\textquotedblright{}

\textbf{Where it comes from.} It is not really a preposition. It is the old present participle of \emph{durar}, \textquotedblleft{}to last\textquotedblright{} — so it once meant \textquotedblleft{}lasting.\textquotedblright{} \emph{Durante dos horas} was \textquotedblleft{}two hours lasting,\textquotedblright{} an absolute phrase that hardened into a fixed word once speakers stopped hearing the verb inside it.

Latin \emph{durare} is \textbf{hard} — \emph{durus} — and it is still visible in English \textbf{durable}, \textbf{duration} and \textbf{endure}. To last is to be hard enough to.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
\emph{Durante} answers \emph{how long}, where \emph{cuándo} answers \emph{when}. Worth a moment's care: English \textquotedblleft{}for\textquotedblright{} stretches over both a length of time and a recipient, and \emph{durante} only ever covers the length.

That completes the chapter's four moves. You can describe an experience now: how it felt, what you hope for next, how it measured against something else, and how long it lasted.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{durante dos horas}
  \item which question it answers — \emph{how long}, not \emph{when}
  \item an experience of yours with a length attached
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What was \emph{durante} before it was a preposition? (The present participle of \emph{durar} — \textquotedblleft{}lasting.\textquotedblright{}) What does Latin \emph{durus} mean, and which English words carry it? (Hard; \textbf{durable}, \textbf{duration}, \textbf{endure}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
